topic: Unit 4: Personal or Creative Writing and Reading Literary and Non-fiction Texts
subject: english-language

moments.title: The Norman Conquest
moments.body: William defeats Harold at Hastings on 14 October. The English aristocracy is replaced by Norman French speakers. For roughly 300 years, England is trilingual: French for the court and aristocracy, Latin for the church and law, English for the common people.
moments.takeaway: 1066 doesn't kill English — it ranks it. English becomes the language of the conquered.

moments.title: Middle English absorbs French wholesale
moments.body: English borrows around 10,000 French words during this period — government (parliament, justice, court, prison), cuisine (beef, pork, mutton — vs. cow, pig, sheep for the live animals tended by English-speaking peasants), and abstract vocabulary. English also sheds most case endings and complicated gender — possibly accelerated by contact with Norse and French.
moments.takeaway: The Walter Scott observation (Ivanhoe, 1819) about animal/meat names is a real and revealing pattern.

moments.title: Statute of Pleading
moments.body: English is restored as the language of the law courts. Parliament is opened in English in 1362. Chaucer writes The Canterbury Tales (begun c. 1387) in English — and the choice itself is a political statement.
moments.takeaway: English's recovery is incomplete and slow. Latin and French persist in law and church well past 1500.

now.title: A hybrid language
now.body: Modern English vocabulary is roughly 26% Germanic, 29% French, 29% Latin, 6% Greek, and the rest borrowed from everywhere. We have layered synonyms (ask/question/interrogate, kingly/royal/regal) that map onto register. English's openness to loanwords — without an academy to police them — is a Norman inheritance.
now.open_questions: Was Middle English creolised? Some linguists (Bailey and Maroldt, 1977) argued English was a Norse/French/English creole; the mainstream view treats it as heavy contact-induced simplification but not full creolisation.

reflection: If you complain about French loanwords in English, you're complaining about a thousand years of English. The hybrid is the language.
